list.listitem: Erysipelas is characterized by acute inflammatory plaques that are raised above the level of the surrounding skin, with a clear line of demarcation between involved and uninvolved tissue. Fever, lymphangitis, adenopathy, and leukocytosis are commonly seen. C
Ancillary tests including needle aspiration, skin biopsy, and blood culture are not commonly needed for immunocompetent patients to establish the diagnosis. C

Penicillin is the treatment of choice for mild to moderate infection. If staphylococcal infection is suspected, a penicillinase-resistant semisynthetic penicillin (ie, dicloxacillin), first-generation cephalosporin, or treatment active against community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus should be selected. B
Consider prophylactic antibiotics for patients with recurrent episodes. B

background.definition: Erysipelas is an acute superficial cellulitis with prominent dermal lymphatic involvement, chiefly characterized by a peripherally spreading hot, bright red, edematous, brawny, infiltrated, and sharply circumscribed plaque with a raised indurated border that is demarcated from normal skin. Key characteristics are that it is raised and sharply demarcated with an indurated "peau d'orange" appearance.

list.listitem: The incidence of erysipelas increased from 1.9 (95% CI, 1.6-2.1) per 1000 patients in 1994 to 2.5 per 1000 patients (95% CI, 2.2-2.7) in 2004.

The incidence of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in patients with erysipelas or cellulitis of the lower extremities range from 0 to 15%. Given the low overall incidence of DVT, routine prophylactic anticoagulation is not indicated in low risk patients. However, DVT should still be considered in patients with high pretest probability or other thromboembolic risk factors.

Erysipelas is a bacterial infection. Three species of streptococci are found: Streptococcus pyogenes (group A) in 58% to 67%; Streptococcus agalactiae (group B) in 3% to 9%; and Streptococcus dysgalactiae sp. equisimilis (groups C and G) in 14% to 25% of the patients.
In some patients, other bacteria are found that may or may not be associated with streptococci, such as Staphylococcus aureus in 10% to 17% and Pseudomonas aeruginosa and enterobacteria in 5% to 50%.
Bacterial inoculation into an area of skin trauma is the usual inciting event, although this may not be clear from the history.

Soft tissue swelling, erythema, warmth, and pain increase as the infection spreads locally through the cutaneous lymphatics. Regional adenopathy and skin streaking may also be seen due to lymphatic involvement.
Bacteremia is uncommon but may occur more in chronically ill or immunocompromised patients.
Diagnosis of erysipelas is based on the association of an acute inflammatory plaque with fever, lymphangitis, adenopathy, and leukocytosis. C

Erysipelas is distinguished clinically from other forms of cutaneous infection by the following two features: Lesions are raised above the level of the surrounding skin and there is a clear line of demarcation between involved and uninvolved tissue. C

Ancillary tests such as needle aspirations, skin biopsies, and blood cultures are not commonly needed to establish the diagnosis due to the characteristic clinical appearance. These tests may be helpful in patients with diabetes mellitus, malignancy, immunodeficiency, or other predisposing factors. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Lacks the warmth, constitutional symptoms, and pain of erysipelas; itching prominent
Typically unilateral dermatomal distribution; varying stages of lesions, not plaques
Raised borders or vesicles lacking; confined to joints, not spreading
Raised borders lacking; usually slower spread and less violaceous appearance
Slow moving; usually involves hands and forearms; throbbing but not as painful as erysipelas
Lacks warmth, redness, tenderness, and constitutional symptoms of erysipelas

list.listitem: Most patients have a predisposing risk factor for soft tissue infection such as chronic leg ulcers, venous insufficiency, dermatophyte infection, lymphatic circulation disorders in particular lymphedema, or other skin trauma.
Systemic factors associated with increased risk for erysipelas, include obesity, diabetes mellitus, CVD, alcoholism and smoking.
Local erythema, tissue swelling, and pain may precede the development of fever by 2 to 3 days.
Erysipelas begins as an erythematous patch that progresses to a fiery red, indurated, painful, raised, sharply demarcated plaque with advancing margins.
The 2 key distinguishing characteristics are that the lesions are raised and sharply demarcated from surrounding tissue.

Fever and malaise are seen in approximately 70% of patients and may persist for days despite appropriate antibiotic therapy. Signs of inflammation may still be present after 10 or more days of appropriate antibiotic therapy.

Generally, no diagnostic tests are needed due to the characteristic clinical appearance. Blood cultures are positive in a minority of patients but may be of higher yield in immunocompromised patients.

Signs and symptoms of systemic toxicity (fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, or hypotension) may suggest a deeper soft tissue infection. In these instances additional laboratory workup may be helpful, including a CBC, CRP, and assessment for sepsis (vital signs, electrolytes). Also consider an alternate diagnosis (cellulitis including staphylococcal disease) in these patients. Cellulitis Carbuncle, furuncle and other skin abscess

Benzyl penicillin and procaine penicillin (2 million units [MU] twice a day in adults) are the antibiotics of choice for mild to moderate erysipelas. For patients with severe disease surgical debridement and vancomyin + piperacillin/tazobactam are recommended by IDSA guidelines (2014). C
Clindamycin may be suitable alternatives in those allergic to penicillin, unless streptococci or staphylococci resistant to these agents are common in the community. C

Adding a tapering dose of prednisolone (30 mg orally once daily tapered over 8 days to 5 mg orally once daily) to IV antibiotic therapy in hospitalized nondiabetic patients with erysipelas produces a modest benefit in reducing symptoms and hospitalization time. B

Benzyl penicillin and procaine penicillin (2 million units [MU] twice a day in adults) are the antibiotics of choice for mild to moderate erysipelas. For patients with severe disease, surgical debridement and vancomyin + piperacillin/tazobactam are recommended by IDSA guidelines (2014).
Other options for mild to moderate erysipelas recommended by IDSA guidelines include ceftriaxone, cefazolin or clindamycin.

Previous evidence from Europe suggests that oral roxithromycin 150 mg twice a day is an effective and well-tolerated treatment for erysipelas in adult hospitalized patients (not available in the United States). However, macrolide resistance among group A streptococci (the predominant pathogen in erysipelas) is increasing in the United States.

Recent European studies suggest that taking oral penicillin V (250 mg orally twice daily) for 6 months after an episode of cellulitis of the leg or for 12 months after recurrent cellulitis of the leg may reduce further attacks, however, further studies are needed on this topic.

Treatment with sequencial IV / oral moxifloxacin as monotherapy once daily was proven to be safe and clinically comparable to oral amoxicillin/clavulanate three times daily for complicated skin infections.
Daptomycin 4 mg/kg intravenous once daily appeared to be effective and safe for treating cellulitis/erysipelas.
Pristinamycin could be an oral first-line alternative to the standard IV-followed-by-oral penicillin regimen used to treat erysipelas in hospitalized adults (not yet available in the United States).

Tedizolid phosphate (an oxazolidinone antibacterial) 200 mg orally daily for 6 days may be a reasonable alternative to linezolid. A randomised blind phase 3 study has confirmed non-inferiority of this regime to linezolid 600 mg twice daily for 10 days.

Prednisolone (30 mg orally once daily tapered over 8 days to 5 mg orally once daily) added to IV antibiotic therapy in hospitalized nondiabetiic patients with erysipelas produces a modest benefit in reducing symptom duration and hospitalization time.
See chapters on cellulitis and skin abscesses for further information on appropriate drug selection when deeper skin and soft tissue infection are suspected.
Topical antibiotics such as mupirocin are not recommended for the treatment of erysipelas.

A Cochrane review included 6 trials with 573 patients with cellulitis and erysipelas with treatment duration of 6 to 18 months. Recurrence, incidence and time to next episode improved with antibiotic preventive treatment compared to placebo. However these preventive effects of antibiotics diminished after discontinuation. The risk of cellulitis recurrence was decreased by 69% with anitbiotic prophylaxis (n = 513; p = 0.007; CI 0.13-0.72).

A recent sytematic review and meta-analysis for cellulitis and erysipelas, with 43 studies and 5999 patients did not support superiority of any 1 antibiotic or any advantage of antibiotics with activity against MRSA.
Sodium selenite application in combination with physical therapy may be useful as prophylaxis against erysipelas in patients with secondary lymphedema.

Effectiveness of selenium in preventing acute inflammatory episodes (AIEs) in lymphedema remains inconclusive. It seems reasonable to emphasize importance of foot care as well as care of the arm in patients with lymphedema for preventing infection.
Consider hospitalization for the very young or very old, homeless patients, and those with diabetes, obesity, or immunocompromised states.

Consider hospitalization and additional antibiotic coverage for staphylococcal infection in patients with hypotension and/or an elevated serum creatinine level, low serum bicarbonate, elevated serum creatinine phosphokinase level (2-3 times the upper limit of normal), marked left shift, or a CRP level higher than 13 mg/L.
Erysipelas has a propensity to recur since it can produce lymphatic abnormalities. One prospective cohort study found that 29% of people with erysipelas had a recurrent episode within 3 years. B

Prophylactic antibiotics may reduce future attacks of cellulitis or erysipelas in people with previous episodes. Uncertainty exists regarding who is most likely to benefit or which antibiotics, doses, and durations of treatment are most likely to be beneficial. B
Diagnostic strategies and treatment options are similar in children and adults; antibiotic dosing should reflect the child's weight and age.
Although some studies have shown equivalent or slightly more activity against streptococci of fluoroquinolones compared with penicillin, they are not recommended for use in children.
